ASSUMPTION: MiLB-translation | Recurrence: promotions happen repeatedly, but the readiness decision is rarely driven by stats alone. Defense, health, 40-man status, and development goals likely dominate, so a stat-translation tool may address a minor input.
ASSUMPTION: MiLB-translation | Data and timing: public MiLB stats are lawful and timely, but the public tracking depth varies by level and is unverified. Any park or league adjustments must use only information available on the decision date, with no end-of-season factors.
ASSUMPTION: MiLB-translation | Actionability: uncertainty bands only matter if staff would change a promotion date or pick a different player. If bands are always wide, the tool shows "we don't know" without changing anything.
ASSUMPTION: MiLB-translation | Testability: a retrospective test is possible. Compare a rolling-origin forecast of next-period MLB performance against a baseline such as regressed prior-season MLB-equivalent projections or a public translation. Judge it on calibration and error, not on anecdotes. Selection bias is a risk because only promoted players have MLB outcomes.
ASSUMPTION: MiLB-translation | Alternatives: public projection systems and translation methods already exist, and sophisticated clubs likely have internal versions using richer private data. A public-data version is at most a baseline.
ASSUMPTION: MiLB-translation | Looks useful but isn't: polished dashboards with confidence bands and in-sample fits on past call-ups. Back-fitted translation factors and hindsight park or league effects also look strong without helping.

ASSUMPTION: Roster-ledger | Recurrence: the decisions recur and the rules are real constraints, so the problem is plausible. The question is whether errors occur, since a rules-literate operations staffer may already prevent them.
ASSUMPTION: Roster-ledger | Data: rules and many transactions are public, but exact option-year counts, service time, and injured-list edge cases may not be fully reconstructable from public logs. A tool that is wrong about eligibility is worse than a spreadsheet maintained by someone with authoritative internal records.
ASSUMPTION: Roster-ledger | Actionability: a warning only helps if it arrives earlier than staff already know. If the answer is "someone would have checked this anyway," the value is only reliability.
ASSUMPTION: Roster-ledger | Testability: public data supports only a weak test. Replay past transactions to see how often a rule-constrained move was made late or missed. Private error logs would be needed for a true baseline, which is a simple manual checklist.
ASSUMPTION: Roster-ledger | Alternatives: spreadsheets, league-office clearance, and internal club systems very likely already do this. Parity at best.
ASSUMPTION: Roster-ledger | Looks useful but isn't: a polished calendar of deadlines that duplicates what staff already track, with no count of avoided errors.

ASSUMPTION: Return-to-play | Recurrence: injured-list placements recur, but each case is individual. Public IL data is sparse on diagnosis, severity, and treatment, so comparables may be too coarse to be informative.
ASSUMPTION: Return-to-play | Data: public IL logs are lawful, but injury labels are often vague or delayed, and players' later performance depends on team-chosen workloads. Only information known at placement time may be used, so leakage from later reports must be excluded.
ASSUMPTION: Return-to-play | Actionability: a public-data distribution of days missed could set roster contingency expectations. It must not override medical judgment, and medical staff with private information have little reason to defer to it.
ASSUMPTION: Return-to-play | Testability: retrospective evaluation is possible. Predict days missed at placement time and compare against a baseline such as the league-wide median by broad injury category. Small sample sizes within categories will limit precision.
ASSUMPTION: Return-to-play | Alternatives: clubs with internal medical databases and vendors likely already do this better. Public writers also publish injury-duration summaries.
ASSUMPTION: Return-to-play | Looks useful but isn't: wide distributions presented as precise timelines, or comparable searches that retrieve a few cases and feel like evidence. Any version using private Cubs medical data in a shared tool would be a compliance concern.

ASSUMPTION: Pitch-predictability | Recurrence: pregame planning recurs. The problem is plausible because predictable sequencing is exploitable, but pitch choice already responds to batter-specific plans, so a count/previous-pitch model may miss the actual reasons.
ASSUMPTION: Pitch-predictability | Data: public pitch-by-pitch data is lawful and available after each game, which supports a self-audit before the next start. The model must be fitted only on past games.
ASSUMPTION: Pitch-predictability | Actionability: a pitcher who is "predictable" can only be told to vary. Unpredictability that sacrifices the best pitch may be worse. Predictability does not equal exploitability unless hitters demonstrably do better when it holds.
ASSUMPTION: Pitch-predictability | Testability: fit the predictability model on early data, then test whether higher predictability correlates with worse outcomes in later data, versus a baseline such as pitch-mix frequency alone. Confounding by pitcher quality and batter strength is likely.
ASSUMPTION: Pitch-predictability | Alternatives: public leaderboards, analysts' spreadsheets, and internal pitching groups probably already include this. Parity at best.
ASSUMPTION: Pitch-predictability | Looks useful but isn't: a high-accuracy classifier. Predictable pitch types, such as fastballs in 0-2 counts or common patterns, may be optimal anyway. A high accuracy score then proves nothing about exploitability.

ASSUMPTION: Context-normalization | Recurrence: minor league evaluators face the problem repeatedly, but it overlaps heavily with MiLB-translation. A rule-regime adjustment is one input to a translation model, not a separate product.
ASSUMPTION: Context-normalization | Data: public league-season stats and rule-change dates are lawful. Effects from rule changes such as automated zones or the pitch clock are confounded with player age, promotion patterns, and the league's talent mix. Using a rule effect estimated after the fact would be hindsight.
ASSUMPTION: Context-normalization | Actionability: the adjustment might alter a promotion date or a prospect comparison, but only if the adjustment is large relative to its error. Small samples per league-season may make the adjustment noisier than the unadjusted line.
ASSUMPTION: Context-normalization | Testability: compare adjusted versus unadjusted stats as predictors of next-level performance, using only information available at the time. The baseline is raw stats with a simple league-average adjustment.
ASSUMPTION: Context-normalization | Alternatives: public park factors and league adjustments exist, and clubs with private tracking data likely do richer normalization.
ASSUMPTION: Context-normalization | Looks useful but isn't: elaborate adjustment factors that change little in rankings, or ones refit each year so they appear to fit.

ASSUMPTION: Bullpen-forecast | Recurrence: the decision recurs daily, and relievers' availability affects pinch-hit and platoon timing. But the opposing manager's choices often depend on warm-up and injury information that is not public.
ASSUMPTION: Bullpen-forecast | Data: box scores with pitch counts are public and available the next morning, so the forecast can be built without hindsight. Rest rules are inferred from patterns. Unobservable factors such as warm-ups and minor injuries cap accuracy.
ASSUMPTION: Bullpen-forecast | Actionability: only useful if the forecast changes the lineup or pinch-hit timing. Staff may already track available arms, and a forecast that says "probably unavailable" might not change anything.
ASSUMPTION: Bullpen-forecast | Testability: strong. Predict each opponent reliever's availability from prior days and compare against a naive rule, such as "no pitching on a third consecutive day or after more than N pitches." Evaluate it by log loss. Then test separately whether Cubs decisions would have changed.
ASSUMPTION: Bullpen-forecast | Alternatives: advance scouts, public bullpen-usage trackers, and club spreadsheets already do this. Fantasy and public sites publish similar availability estimates.
ASSUMPTION: Bullpen-forecast | Looks useful but isn't: a good availability forecast with no link to a Cubs decision. Accuracy is inflated because most relievers are obviously available or unavailable, so easy cases dominate.

ASSUMPTION: Set-wide blind spot | All six assume that information is the bottleneck. None test whether Cubs staff already have the information, or whether decisions are limited by communication, trust, authority, or time.
ASSUMPTION: Set-wide blind spot | Five of six rely on public data, which sophisticated clubs also hold, so the realistic outcome is parity. None names a source of advantage that rivals lack, such as private data the club may lawfully hold, faster internal routing, or better adoption.
ASSUMPTION: Set-wide blind spot | None includes a baseline cost: staff time, maintenance, and the opportunity cost relative to a spreadsheet. None measures value in runs, wins, or dollars, and the lines of evidence are mostly speculation without a size estimate.
ASSUMPTION: Set-wide blind spot | Uncovered users and decisions: amateur draft and international scouting, contract and free-agent valuation, in-game defensive positioning, player health and workload management by the performance staff, and coach–player communication. The set is heavily weighted toward analyst-facing prediction and under-weights operational and human-process decisions.
ASSUMPTION: Set-wide blind spot | Common failure modes: hindsight leakage in retrospective tests, small samples with many comparisons, selection bias (outcomes seen only for chosen players), confounding by team strategy, adoption failure, and polished tools that do not change decisions.
IDEA: Decision-impact audit | Before building any of the six, run a one-month process audit with a few staff to list which decisions were made, what information was used, and what they would change. Rank candidates by the share of decisions where the tool would alter a choice, using a spreadsheet prototype and a naive baseline.
IDEA: Prototype-first MiLB model | Merge MiLB-translation and Context-normalization into one rolling-origin evaluation harness on public data, scored against a naive baseline for calibration. Build the interface only if it beats the baseline out of sample.

ASSUMPTION: CallUp (problem) Promotion calls recur every season, but the binding constraints are often roster spots, 40-man and option status, and need, not translated-stat accuracy. A better estimate may not change who is promoted.
ASSUMPTION: CallUp (data) Public MiLB stats are lawful, and end-of-day box scores are usable without hindsight. Level-specific tracking coverage is uneven, and league rule and ball changes can break the translation. Training and testing must be strictly time-split.
ASSUMPTION: CallUp (action) Staff would act differently only if the uncertainty band changes a decision at the margin. If the call is made on makeup, defense, health, or 40-man logistics, the band is decorative.
ASSUMPTION: CallUp (test) A retrospective test is feasible: compare projected versus realized MLB outcomes for historical call-ups against a naive baseline, such as the prior-year MLB-equivalent or a level-average regression. The sample is small and outcomes are noisy, so calibration of the bands is testable but decision value is not.
ASSUMPTION: CallUp (alternatives) Translation methods are widely published, and public sites and prospect-ranking systems already exist. Clubs likely hold better private models, so a public-data version is parity at best.
ASSUMPTION: CallUp (looks useful) A polished band chart that reproduces consensus projections looks rigorous. A tool that was never scored against a naive baseline, or that tunes translation factors on seasons it is then tested on, would look useful and add nothing.

UNKNOWN: CallUp cubs_internal_translation_models
UNKNOWN: CallUp share_of_promotions_where_performance_estimate_was_the_binding_factor
ASSUMPTION: RosterLedger (problem) The problem is real and recurs: option years, minimum optional-assignment durations, DFA and Rule 5 deadlines. The errors are probably rare and the staff probably rules-literate, so the cost avoided per season is unknown.
ASSUMPTION: RosterLedger (data) Public transaction logs do not fully reconstruct option status, injured-list time, service time, or rule changes. Without the club's own authoritative records the ledger may be wrong, and a ledger that is confidently wrong is worse than none.
ASSUMPTION: RosterLedger (action) The warnings would change timing of moves, but only if they arrive earlier than existing reminders do. If staff already track deadlines, the added warning has no value.
ASSUMPTION: RosterLedger (test) Public data cannot show avoided errors. The only available test is back-casting: replay historical public transactions and check whether the ledger flags known constraint-driven outcomes. Missed-deadline counts are not publicly observable.
ASSUMPTION: RosterLedger (alternatives) A spreadsheet plus a baseball-operations staffer, league transaction systems, and existing club operations software probably cover this. Sophisticated clubs almost certainly have it.
ASSUMPTION: RosterLedger (looks useful) A dashboard populated from public transactions looks complete while omitting private contract and service data. Demos that show clean dates for ordinary players hide the edge cases where errors actually happen.

ASSUMPTION: ReturnToPlay (problem) Injury timelines recur, but the decision is dominated by diagnosis and surgeon and medical-staff judgment. Public injured-list labels are coarse and are not medical data.
ASSUMPTION: ReturnToPlay (data) Public IL transactions give dates and loose injury descriptions, and are lawful. Descriptions are sometimes vague or reported after the fact, and many injured-list stints are roster-management artifacts rather than health. Using public data keeps it away from private medical records, but a tool used by medical staff would tempt them to mix the two.
ASSUMPTION: ReturnToPlay (action) A distribution of days missed could inform roster contingency timing. It should not set the medical return date, and a naive comparable could anchor staff on a misleading median.
ASSUMPTION: ReturnToPlay (test) Testable retrospectively: predict days missed from public comparables versus a baseline of a simple per-injury-type median, using only information available when the player was placed on the IL. Post-return performance has heavy selection and sample-size problems.
ASSUMPTION: ReturnToPlay (alternatives) Public injury trackers and league databases exist. Clubs' internal medical databases are almost certainly richer, so the public version would be a weak benchmark.
ASSUMPTION: ReturnToPlay (looks useful) Wide, honest-looking distributions look informative but are too diffuse to change a decision. Retrofitting injury categories after the outcome is known would inflate apparent accuracy.

UNKNOWN: ReturnToPlay accuracy_vs_median_baseline
UNKNOWN: ReturnToPlay cubs_internal_medical_database_capability
ASSUMPTION: SequenceAudit (problem) Pregame game-plan design recurs daily. It is unproven that sequence predictability from count and prior pitch is exploitable independent of pitch quality, and predictable sequencing is not necessarily bad if pitch quality is high.
ASSUMPTION: SequenceAudit (data) Public pitch-by-pitch data is lawful and available after each game. Features like count, previous pitch, and batter handedness are known at decision time. Fitting and testing on the same season leaks.
ASSUMPTION: SequenceAudit (action) A pitcher or catcher would change mixes only if a predictability finding is stable and the alternative sequence costs nothing in pitch quality. Otherwise the finding yields no action.
ASSUMPTION: SequenceAudit (test) Testable: out-of-sample next-pitch prediction versus a count-only baseline, then whether predictability correlates with outcomes after controlling for pitch quality. The causal claim that reducing predictability lowers runs is not testable from observational public data.
ASSUMPTION: SequenceAudit (alternatives) Pitching staffs and clubs likely already have this internally, with richer tracking, and public pitch-mix tools exist. The value is parity.
ASSUMPTION: SequenceAudit (looks useful) A high next-pitch accuracy score looks alarming but mostly reflects the base rate of fastballs in certain counts. Without a count-only baseline, entropy charts look insightful while adding nothing.

UNKNOWN: SequenceAudit evidence_linking_sequence_entropy_to_run_prevention
ASSUMPTION: LeagueNorm (problem) Evaluators repeatedly compare prospects across leagues and parks, so the decision recurs. Rule regimes such as the automated strike zone and pitch clock differ by level and season, which is a real confound.
ASSUMPTION: LeagueNorm (data) Public MiLB stats and park information are lawful. Rule-regime effects are estimated from few league-seasons, so effect estimates are confounded with talent and call-up selection. Season-level adjustments computed with data from after the decision date are hindsight.
ASSUMPTION: LeagueNorm (action) Evaluators would discount or boost certain stat lines. Action only changes if the adjustments are large relative to scout judgment and noise.
ASSUMPTION: LeagueNorm (test) Testable against a baseline of raw stats or standard league-and-park-adjusted stats: does the adjusted metric better predict next-level performance, using only data available at the time? Small samples and roster churn limit power.
ASSUMPTION: LeagueNorm (alternatives) Public sites partly normalize already, and clubs likely have private league adjustments. It overlaps heavily with CallUp and should perhaps be merged with it.
ASSUMPTION: LeagueNorm (looks useful) Large, tidy-looking adjustment factors fitted on few league-seasons overfit and look authoritative. A tool that only reproduces the public park factors looks complete but adds nothing.

UNKNOWN: LeagueNorm public_milb_park_factor_quality
ASSUMPTION: BullpenForecast (problem) Late-game matchup planning recurs nightly, but opposing availability is often known or guessed by experienced staff. The decision it changes, such as holding a pinch hitter, is narrow.
ASSUMPTION: BullpenForecast (data) Public box scores give appearances and pitch counts after games, which is lawful and available before the next game. Warm-up activity, injury, and fatigue are not observable. Pregame information is limited to prior games, so live in-game availability is not covered.
ASSUMPTION: BullpenForecast (action) The manager would adjust lineup order or bench use only if forecasts shift a real decision, which is rare. Usage is increasingly set by opposing front offices, not stable manager habits.
ASSUMPTION: BullpenForecast (test) Testable by predicting which relievers appear versus a naive rule, such as unavailable after pitching back-to-back or after a high pitch count. Forecast accuracy is testable, but the effect on Cubs win probability is not.
ASSUMPTION: BullpenForecast (alternatives) Advance scouts, public bullpen-usage trackers, and club-internal usage models already cover this. Sophisticated clubs have richer data, including private rest rules.
ASSUMPTION: BullpenForecast (looks useful) Probability tables for each reliever look precise, but if they merely restate who pitched yesterday they provide nothing beyond a naive rule. Accuracy is easy to report on trivial cases like relievers who clearly are unavailable.

IDEA: Merged Prospect Evaluation Backtest Harness: combine CallUp and LeagueNorm into one point-in-time evaluator. It uses only data available at each historical decision date, scores translated projections against raw and standard park-adjusted baselines, and publishes a kill criterion in advance.
IDEA: Decision-Level Baseline Audit: before building anything, have staff log how each recurring decision was actually made and what information was used for a season. This tests which of these six tools would change a choice at all, and costs far less than building them.
IDEA: Pre-registered Forecast Ledger: record each forecast, such as bullpen usage, promotion readiness, or injury timeline, with confidence before the outcome, and score it against naive rules. This turns RosterLedger, BullpenForecast, and ReturnToPlay into testable claims.
